content: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the presence of endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity. It affects approximately 7% to 10% of women of reproductive age and commonly manifests as pelvic pain or infertility. The pelvic pain may present as dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation), dyspareunia (pain during intercourse), or non-cyclic pelvic pain. Historically, a combination of estrogens and progestagens was used to induce a state of pseudopregnancy, thereby alleviating symptoms. However, progestagens alone or anti-progestagens have been explored as alternative treatments due to their lower cost and potentially more favorable side effect profiles. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of progestagens and anti-progestagens in managing pain associated with endometriosis. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing these treatments to other interventions, placebo, or no treatment. The search strategy was updated in 2011, and six new studies were added, bringing the total number of included studies to 13. The newly included studies assessed progestagens in various comparisons, including placebo, danazol, oral or subdermal contraceptives, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues, and other drugs. Other studies compared the anti-progestagen gestrinone with danazol, GnRH analogues, or itself. Medroxyprogesterone acetate (100 mg daily) was found to be more effective than placebo in reducing all symptoms of endometriosis up to 12 months of follow-up. However, this treatment was associated with significantly higher rates of acne and edema compared to placebo. There was no evidence of a difference in efficacy between dydrogesterone and placebo. Depot administration of progestagens did not demonstrate superior efficacy compared to other treatments, such as low-dose oral contraceptives or leuprolide acetate, and was associated with more adverse effects. Oral progestagens did not show a clear benefit over other medical treatments at six months of follow-up, and side effects such as amenorrhea and abnormal bleeding were more frequently reported in the progestagen group. Regarding anti-progestagens, there was no evidence that gestrinone was more effective than danazol. However, the GnRH analogue leuprorelin significantly improved dysmenorrhea compared to gestrinone, though it was associated with a higher incidence of hot flushes. In conclusion, the evidence supporting the use of progestagens and anti-progestagens for pain management in endometriosis is limited. Further research is needed to establish their efficacy and safety profiles in comparison to other treatment options.
